He rules over the oblations of men, the offerings prepared with the *iḷā* hymn.
May he protect us from the malice of Varuṇa, from the malice of the great god.
They praise Agni, the invoker, the bestower of wealth; they have appointed him as the beloved, most wise messenger, they have appointed him as the bearer of oblations.

The gods, seeking riches, have praised with songs the one who sustains all life, the all-knowing, the adorable sage, the invoker, the delightful one for their protection—seeking riches, they have praised the delightful one with songs.
O Indra, that chariot which you, the impetuous one, lead forward from afar for the winning of the prize—O blameless one, you lead it on; you instantly make it victorious for our desired goal.
O blameless and impetuous one, accept this speech of ours, as you have accepted the speech of the wise.
Hear us, O Indra, you who are to be honored by men in every battle when the call to arms is raised; you are with the men for the sake of swift victory.

You who, with heroes, win the light of heaven, and with sages, overcome for the prize—him, the powerful one, the masters have sought to win, like a prize-winning steed, like a swift courser laden with nourishment.

For you, O wondrous one, cause the bull-like skin to swell; you ward off every hostile mortal, O hero, you exclude the mortal foe. And this, O Indra, I shall declare to Heaven, to Rudra who is self-glorious, to Mitra and Varuṇa—this far-reaching praise, this far-reaching prayer for their great mercy.
We desire you, O Indra, as our friend for our protection—the all-enlivening, victorious ally, the victorious ally in battles. May our prayer prevail in every conflict;
for no enemy can strike you down, but you strike him down—you strike down every enemy.
Bend down the overweening pride of every man with your most sharpened kindling-sticks, with your aids that are fierce, with your fierce aids.
Lead us as you did of old, O Hero, whom you consider blameless;
as a bearer, carry us across all [difficulties] of the Pūru people, bearing us hither by your mouth.

I would proclaim this to the future Soma-drop, he who, like one to be invoked, possessing nourishment, stirs the prayer; the demon-slayer stirs the prayer. May he himself drive away from us the scorner with his weapons, the evil-minded one. May the wicked one flow away, may he flow downward like a tiny speck of dust.
May we win that through thoughtful invocation; may we win wealth, O Lord of Wealth, and heroic power—wealth that is delightful, heroic power.
With hymns of praise, let us satisfy the ill-minded one with food;
with true, glorious invocations, let us worship Indra, the one worthy of sacrifice, with glorious invocations.

May Indra come forth to us with his own glorious aids, for the complete removal of the ill-minded; may he shatter the ill-minded. May that [hostile force] which has approached us with its devouring jaws perish by itself.
It shall carry away our distress like a cast-off garment; it shall carry away our wasting fever like a discarded rag.

Come to us, O Indra, with abundant wealth; come by paths that are unobstructed. Go before us on a path free from demons. Be with us in the distance; be with us at home. Protect us from afar and from near at hand with your aids; ever protect us with your aids.
O Indra, may you grant us wealth that overcomes our enemies; may your greatness accompany you, the fierce one, for our great protection, as one seeks the aid of a friend for protection.
O most powerful protector and helper, O immortal, [protect] every chariot;
do not harm anyone other than us, O wielder of the stone, nor anyone who seeks to harm us, O wielder of the stone.
Protect us from calamity, O Indra, you who are well-praised; as a god, you are forever the warder-off of the ill-minded, the slayer of the evil demon, and the protector of a sage such as I.
For thus indeed did the progenitor beget you, O Vasu; he begot you, O Vasu, as the slayer of demons.
O Indra, come to us from afar, as a lord of the people comes to the assemblies, as a king comes to his home; we, providing the sacrificial food, invoke you at the pressing of the juice,
like sons invoking their father for the winning of booty— invoking the most bountiful one for the winning of booty.
Drink the Soma pressed by the stones, O Indra; drink it as it is poured from the vessel, like a thirsty bull drinking fresh water.
It is for your exhilaration, for you who are beloved, and for your most powerful sustenance.
May they bring you hither, as the bay horses bring the Sun, even as all bring the Sun.

He found the treasure hidden in the cave of heaven, like the embryo of a plant wrapped within a stone, within the infinite stone— the best of the Aṅgirasas, desiring to win it as one wins a stall of cattle with the thunderbolt.
Indra threw open the doors that enclosed the food, the food that was shut away.
Grasping the thunderbolt in his two hands, Indra—sharpening it like a blade, making it keen and of iron for the hurling—whetted it for the slaying of the serpent.
Enveloped in power, in strengths, O Indra, and in majesty.
Like a carpenter felling a tree, you hew down the forest trees; like an axe, you hew them down.
O Indra, you have released the rivers to flow at will toward the ocean, like chariots seeking booty, like chariots racing for the prize.
From here they have yoked themselves for aid, toward a single, inexhaustible goal.

Like milch-cows yielding all things for mankind, yielding all things for the people; these mortals, seeking wealth, have fashioned this speech for you, as a skillful craftsman fashions a chariot— they have fashioned you for favor, O Sage, adorning you like a noble steed for the sake of booty in the contests.

Like a steed for strength, for the winning of riches— for the winning of all riches— O Indra, you shattered ninety forts for Pūru Divodāsa, the great donor, O dancer; with your thunderbolt, O dancer, you struck down Śambara from the mountain for the sake of the donor Atithigva, you the fierce one.

Distributing great riches by his might, all riches by his might— Indra, the one with a hundred aids, protected the Aryan sacrificer in battles, in all contests for light, in the struggles for booty. Governing for Manu, he subdued the lawless and made the black skin subject to him.
Like one providing skill, he burns away everything that thirsts; he burns away the leper.
The Sun, having been born with power, has cast forth his wheel; at the onset of the day, the ruddy one steals away the voice; as the sovereign lord, he steals it away.
When Uśanas came from afar for protection, O Sage.
Overpowering all blessings like Manu, he overcomes all with his days. O you of heroic deeds, destroyer of forts, protect us with your powerful guardians through our new hymns of praise.
Praised by the Divodāsas, O Indra, may you increase in strength like the sky grows by its days.
For to Indra has Dyaus, the Asura, bowed down; for Indra has the great Earth bowed with her vast expanses, in the winning of glory, with her vast expanses.
All the gods, acting in unison, have placed Indra at their head.
For Indra let all the human libations be offered, the human offerings.
For at all libations, those who desire the bull urge you on—the one and the same—each separately, seeking to win the light of heaven, each separately.
We set you, like a ship that carries us across, at the pole of our strength;
men clarify Indra with sacrifices, men clarify Indra with hymns of praise.
Couples seeking your aid have exerted themselves for you, O Indra, as they release the streams to win the stall of cattle; may they overcome the obstacles, O Indra, as they release the streams.
When you bring together two people—one seeking cattle, the other seeking heaven—you, O Indra, manifest the bull-like thunderbolt that accompanies you, the companion that accompanies you.
The Pūrus have known this heroic deed of yours, O Indra, when you overthrew the autumnal fortresses; overcoming them, you overthrew them.
You chastised that mortal who would not sacrifice, O Indra, Lord of Might;
you won back the great earth and these waters, rejoicing in these waters.

From the beginning they have celebrated this heroic deed of yours, O Bull, in the exhilarations of Soma, when you, being implored, protected those who sought your friendship; when you protected them, you brought success to these men in the battles, for you are their helpers.
Desiring glory, they won one river after another; desiring glory, they won them.
And may he be pleased with us at this dawn; take note of this hymn and the oblation through our invocations, at the winning of the light through our invocations.
O Indra, wielder of the thunderbolt, when you, the bull, intend to slay the adversaries, listen to this prayer of mine, the most recent of this worshipper, the most recent of all.

O Indra, growing strong and well-disposed toward us, O many-born hero, slay with your thunderbolt that mortal who acts as an enemy, that mortal who seeks to harm us. Listen, you who are most renowned! Let ill-will be swept away like a mishap on a journey; let all ill-will be dispelled.
O Maghavan, with you as our protector, O Indra, may we overcome those who attack us and conquer those who seek to harm us in the ancient struggle for wealth.
On this most immediate day, speak now in favor of the one who presses the soma;
at this sacrifice, may we, seeking booty, distribute the prize won in battle.
In the winning of light, bring [the prize] at the speech of the filler, for those who wake at dawn, in their own direct splendor, for those who have attained their own direct splendor.
Indra slew [the foe] as is known; he is to be praised head by head.
May your gifts be gathered together toward us—auspicious are the gifts of the auspicious one.
That indeed is your ancient food, shining as of old, at the sacrifice where they made you the chooser, the dweller in the abode of *ṛta*; you choose that dwelling.
Proclaim this now and hereafter; they behold it within with their rays.
Verily, Indra is known as the seeker of cattle, the seeker of cattle for those who dwell in kinship.
Now indeed, as in the past, this deed of yours is to be proclaimed—that when you helped the Aṅgirases, O Indra, you opened the stall, you opened the stall.
To them, in the same direction, for us you shall conquer and fight.
Yield up to those who press the Soma every lawless one, even the one who is full of wrath, the lawless one.
When the Hero, with his powers of will, has caused the people to look upon one another as the prize is staked, those seeking glory overcome their foes; seeking glory, they press forward.
To him, in the face of oppression, they sing for life accompanied by progeny through their might; the prayers desire a dwelling-place in Indra, even as the prayers seek the Gods.

O Indra and Parvata, you two who fight from the front, strike down each one who would attack us; strike him down with the thunderbolt, strike him down! May he find a deep abyss that shall swallow him up when he reaches it, far away from us.
O Hero, may you destroy our enemies on every side; may you, the destroyer, crush them from all quarters.
I purify both heaven and earth with cosmic order (*ṛta*); I burn away the great, godless deceivers.
Where the enemies were struck down after being hemmed in, they lay scattered about, crushed at Vailasthāna.
O wielder of the stone, having torn open the heads of the sorceresses, cut them off with your wide-spreading foot, with your great wide-spreading foot.
O Maghavan, strike down the host of these sorceresses.
In the hollow of the *vaila* tree, in the hollow of the great *vaila* tree—
those of whom you have cast off fifty-three with your leaps— that one takes pleasure in the pressed juice; that one truly takes pleasure in it for you.
O Indra, crush Piśāci, the fierce one with tawny-tipped arrows;
strike down every Rākṣasa.
O great Indra, rend asunder [the enemy]; hear us, for heaven has glowed with fear, O wielder of the stone, as if from the heat of the sun, O wielder of the stone.

For you, the most powerful one, advance with your powerful weapons and your fierce [blows]. O hero who slays no men, you are irresistible, O hero, with your thrice-seven warriors, with your thrice-seven warriors.
For the one who presses the juice gains a dwelling of abundance; for the one who presses the juice indeed worships away his enemies—the enemies of the gods, away his enemies.
The one who presses the juice desires to win thousands, he who is chosen for the prize. To the one who presses the juice, Indra gives abundant wealth; he gives abundant wealth.
O Vāyu, let the swift, rushing steeds bring you here to the food, to the first drinking of the Soma, to the first drinking!
May thy *sūnṛtā* (joyful bounty), knowing [us], stand firm after thee.
Come hither with thy chariot drawn by teams of horses, O Vāyu, to give, to give the sacrificial gift.
May the exhilarating drops, O Vāyu, gladden thee—those well-prepared, heaven-reaching draughts made from milk, well-prepared and reaching heaven.

When his powers have been set in motion for the sake of achieving his will, the aids attend upon his skill; the teams come together to bestow gifts, and the prayers address him with devotion—these are the prayers.
Vāyu yokes the two ruddy steeds, Vāyu the two tawny ones; Vāyu yokes the two swift horses to the chariot-pole to draw it, the most excellent at drawing the pole.
Awaken Purandhi, as a lover awakens a sleeping woman.
Make the two worlds visible; clothe the dawns in splendor—clothe the dawns in splendor.
For you, the bright dawns spread out their auspicious garments in the distance, wondrously among your rays—brilliant in your new rays.
For you the cow, yielding milk at all times, milks forth all treasures. From her womb you generated the Maruts; from the womb of heaven [you generated them].
For you the bright, pure, and swift ones, fierce in their exhilarations, have sped toward the nourishment that brings prosperity; they have sped toward the nourishment that brings prosperity.
The thief, seeking to harm, prays to you for fortune in his swift pursuit.

You protect us from every world by your law; you protect us from the realm of the Asuras by your law. O Vāyu, you who are without predecessor, as the first among these pressed Soma juices, you deserve the first draught; you deserve the draught of the pressed juices.
And so, from the people who have offered worship and have turned away [from evil], all the milch-cows yield for you the milk-mixture; they yield the clarified butter, they yield the milk-mixture.
The sacrificial grass is strewn; come to us for the feast with a thousand teams, O Lord of the teams, with hundreds of teams, O Lord of the teams!
For the gods have submitted themselves to you, the god, for your first draught. The pressed juices, rich in sweetness, have stood forth for you; they have stood forth for exhilaration and for wisdom.
For you this Soma flows, purified by the stones, clothing himself in desirable garments as he flows around the vat; clothing himself in bright raiment, he flows.
This portion of yours, O Soma, is offered among the gods for your long life.
O Vāyu, bring your teams; come well-disposed toward us; enjoying [the offering], come well-disposed toward us.
With your teams, by the hundreds and by the thousands, come to our sacrifice for the feast, O Vāyu, to enjoy the oblations.
This is your seasonal portion, accompanied by rays, together with the sun.
Brought by the *adhvaryu* priests, they have been offered; O Vāyu, the bright drops have been offered.
May your chariot, drawn by teams of horses, bring you for our protection, toward the well-placed offerings for your enjoyment, O Vāyu, toward the oblations for your enjoyment.
Drink of the sweet juice, for the first draught has been set apart for you both.
O Vāyu, come with brilliant wealth; and you, Indra, come with wealth.
May our prayers turn you both toward the sacrifices; they have cleansed this vigorous Soma-drop like a swift, prize-winning steed.
Drink of these, showing us favor; come hither to us, O Indra and Vāyu! Drink of the juices pressed by the stones for your exhilaration, O you two givers of booty.
These Soma juices, pressed here in the waters by the *adhvaryu*s, have been offered to you both; O Vāyu, the bright drops have been offered.
These swift ones have been sent forth for you two, across the filter; seeking you, the Soma juices pass through the sheep’s wool, past the fleece.
O Vāyu, pass by those who lie in wait in their multitudes; go to that place where the pressing-stone speaks, and go to the house, O Indra and Vāyu.
The *sūnṛtā* has become visible; ghee flows forth. With a full team you come to the sacrifice; Indra and [Vāyu], you come to the sacrifice.
Here indeed you two carry away the oblation of honey, which the swift ones attend at the *aśvattha* tree; may they be victorious for us—may they be victorious for us.
Together the cows bring forth; barley is ripened. O Vāyu, your milch-cows do not fail; the milch-cows do not fail.

These which are yours, O Vāyu, possessing strength in their arms—these bulls fly within the rivers, swelling greatly, these bulls; even those that are not swift on the desert plain, yet are quick and dwell upon the mountains.
Like the rays of the sun, they are difficult to restrain; they are difficult to restrain by the hands.
Bring forth the highest, great homage, an offering, and a prayer for the two observant ones who are gracious—the most sweet [prayer] for those who are gracious.
Those two sovereign kings, to whom the clarified butter is poured, are praised at every sacrifice.
Now their dominion is not to be assailed from any quarter; their divinity is never to be assailed.
A wider path has been seen for the broad expanse; the course of *ṛta* has been aligned with its rays, the eye with the rays of Bhaga.
The celestial abode of Mitra, Aryaman, and Varuṇa has been beheld.
Then they two bestow great vitality upon the one worthy of speech, great vitality that is to be celebrated.

They attend to Aditi, who possesses light, who sustains the world, and who is full of heaven, day after day, they who are ever-watchful day after day. The Ādityas, lords of the gift, have attained a luminous dominion.
Of these two, Mitra and Varuṇa are the people’s uniter; Aryaman is the people’s uniter.
May this Soma, becoming most auspicious for Mitra and Varuṇa, be a participant in the drinking-feasts, a god among the gods as a participant.
May all the gods, being of one accord, take pleasure in it today. O Kings, fulfill that which we implore you for, since you are upholders of the Eternal Law (Ṛta).
The man who serves Mitra and Varuṇa, him they protect from distress—the liberal mortal from distress. Aryaman guards him who acts uprightly according to the sacred law;
he who honors their law with hymns of praise, he who adorns their law with songs of praise.
Homage to the lofty heaven, to the two worlds, to Mitra, and to the bounteous Varuṇa, the most merciful and bounteous!
Praise Indra and Agni; praise the celestial Aryaman and Bhaga!
Living long, may we be united with progeny; may we be united with the protection of Soma.

Through the protection of the gods, may we, accompanied by Indra and the Maruts, be mindful of our own glory. May Agni, Mitra, and Varuṇa grant us shelter; may the patrons and we ourselves attain that.
We have pressed [the juice] with stones; come hither! These exhilarating Soma-draughts, mixed with milk, are intoxicating; these Soma-draughts are intoxicating.
O Kings who touch the heavens, come hither to us!
These Soma juices, mixed with milk, are for you, O Mitra and Varuna—bright, mixed with milk.
Come here to these drops, the pressed Soma juices mixed with curds—pressed, mixed with curds.
And at the awakening of the dawn, together with the rays of the sun,
the pressed juice is offered for Mitra and Varuṇa to drink— the lovely one, for the sake of the Truth to drink.
Like a cow that yields milk at dawn, they milk that stalk for you with the stones; they milk the Soma with the stones. Come toward us, come hither to us, both of you, for the drinking of the Soma.
O Mitra and Varuṇa, this Soma has been pressed by the men for you; it is pressed for your drinking.
On and on is celebrated the greatness of Pūṣan, the one of mighty birth; the praise of this powerful one does not falter, his hymn does not falter.
Seeking favor, I sing to him who brings aid at hand, the source of bliss—he who, as a vigorous god, has drawn to himself the mind of every man, the vigorous one who has drawn it to himself.
For I urge you forward, O Pūṣan, as one would a swift steed on its course with hymns of praise, so that you may overcome our adversaries; like a camel, carry us across our foes.
Since I, a mortal, call upon you, the god who brings bliss, for friendship, make our songs of praise glorious; in the contests for booty, make them glorious.
O Pūṣan, those who are praiseworthy in your friendship, being wise through their own insight, have enjoyed your protection; indeed, they have enjoyed it through their insight.
Following that most recent team of horses, we seek you for wealth.
O you of wide renown, be gracious; in every contest for booty, be gracious.
O Lord of the Unborn Horses, being gracious and bountiful, come quickly to us for our gain; come to those who seek glory, O Lord of the Unborn Horses!
O Wonder-worker, may we turn you hither with our effective hymns of praise, for I do not disregard you, O glowing Pūṣan, nor do I deny your friendship.
Let there be *śrauṣaṭ*; with my thought I place Agni at the forefront. Now we choose that divine host; we choose Indra and Vāyu.
For when the newest [hymn] has been offered upon the central navel where Vivasvat acts, then may our thoughts go forth toward the gods, even as our thoughts go toward the gods.
When you two, O Mitra and Varuṇa, took that untruth away from the Truth by your own will, by your own will of skill;
then in your dwellings we beheld that which was golden.
Even with our prayers, with the mind, and with our own eyes—with the own eyes of Soma.
O Aśvins, those seeking the gods, like people calling out a hymn, have raised their voices with songs of praise; the living beings have called upon you for their oblations.
O possessors of all wealth, all glories and nourishments rest upon you both. O wonder-workers, the fellies of your golden chariot sprinkle moisture as they move.
O wonder-workers, you have been perceived; you open up the firmament. For you, at the rites of heaven, they harness the chariot-steeds—unblemished steeds at the rites of heaven.
O wonder-workers, your station is upon the seat of the golden chariot. Like two travelers on a path, you traverse the mid-air, directing it straight; you direct the mid-air directly.
O Lords of power, with your powers, favor us by day and by night! May your bounty never fail us; may your bounty never fail us at any time.
O Bull Indra, these Soma drops are for you—the bull-drinkers; they are pressed by the stones, bursting forth, pressed for you, bursting forth.
May they exhilarate you for the sake of giving great and wondrous wealth.
O you who are borne by songs, being praised with hymns, come hither; as one who is gracious, come to us.
O Agni, hear us well! Being praised, you shall speak to the gods who are worthy of sacrifice, to the kings who are worthy of sacrifice.
Since, O Gods, you gave that cow to the Aṅgirases, Aryaman milks her along with the preparer; he knows her as being with me.

May those manly deeds of yours never turn away from us; may your glories not decay, nor may our fortresses decay. Whatever wondrous, immortal, and ever-new sound you have sent forth age after age—O Maruts, bestow that upon us, and that which is difficult to overcome, grant that which is difficult to overcome.

Dadhyañc, the ancient Aṅgiras, Priyamedha, Kaṇva, Atri, and Manu knew my origin; those ancients, including Manu, knew it for me. Their lineage extends to the gods, and our kinships are with them. Following their path, I bow down with my song; I bow down with my song to Indra and Agni.
Let the Hotṛ sacrifice; let the seekers of wood win what is desirable. Bṛhaspati, the seer, sacrifices with bulls—bulls rich in many boons.
We have ourselves grasped the far-reaching song from the mountain.
The one of excellent wisdom has established the non-giving gifts; the one of excellent wisdom has established many dwellings.
O gods who are eleven in heaven, you who are eleven upon the earth, you who dwell in the waters— eleven by your greatness— O gods, may you graciously accept this sacrifice.
To Agni, who sits upon the altar, whose abode is dear, and who shines with beautiful luster—bring forth a nourishing offering to his seat.
Clothe the pure one with my hymn as if with a garment; he whose chariot is light, whose color is bright, and who destroys the darkness.

The twice-born one, whose food is the threefold [sacrifice], hastens toward it; what was consumed grows again within the year. With the tongue of the one, the noble bull wins; with the other, the choice one has stripped the trees.
Both his companions, moving through the darkness, tremble; both mothers cross over toward the infant.
With forward-tongued flames, scattering [the darkness], flowing with thirst, worthy of being approached, impetuous, and increasing the strength of his father—[these steeds] are harnessed.
Seeking release for Manu who acts like a wise man, the swift-runners, leaving black furrows behind, are quick;
diverse, agile, gliding swiftly, and urged by the wind, these fleet horses are yoked.
Then these [flames] of his fly about at will, scattering [the darkness], making the great form of black, monstrous power manifest.
When he has grasped the vast earth, he goes forth panting, thundering, and roaring.
He who bends down over the brown [plants] like one adorning himself, approaches his wives like a bull bellowing aloud.
Displaying his vigor, he adorns his body; like a formidable beast, he is difficult to seize when he has burst forth from the horn.
He, the pervasive one, gathers those who are spread out; even as he is being born, he lies within those who know him eternally.
They grow again and attain divinity; together with their parents, they assume another form.
The long-haired, aged women, having been revived by his roar, stood up again for the sake of the living man, though they had been as if dead.
Releasing them from old age, he goes along roaring, generating vital breath, the supreme, invincible life-force.
Licking the garment upon him, he traverses the wide expanse with his powerful, swift-moving warriors.
Bestowing vigor upon all that moves on feet, licking them constantly, the ruddy one follows her paths day by day.
O Agni, shine among our patrons, you who are like a snorting bull, the master of the house.
You have caused these mother-cows with their calves to glow, flickering about like a coat of mail in battles.
O Agni, may this well-composed prayer be dearer to you than a poorly composed one, even more so than a beloved thought.
With that pure, radiant light of your body which shines forth, O bright one, win wealth for us.
O Agni, grant us a ship with its own oars and feet for our chariot and for our home.
May she carry across our heroes, our liberal patrons, and our people—she who is our protection and our refuge.
O Agni, may Heaven and Earth and the self-praising rivers accept our hymn of praise;
seeking cattle and grain for a long life, may the ruddy dawns grant us what is most excellent.
Truly, that beautiful splendor of the god has been established for the sake of majesty, since he was born from strength.
When he inclines toward it, the prayer succeeds; they have led forth the flowing milch-cows of Truth.
The nourishing, wondrous form dwells eternally in food; a second [form] dwells in the seven auspicious mothers.

The young women brought forth the third [birth] of this bull for milking—the one who possesses tenfold wisdom. When, from the depths of the buffalo’s form, the wise lords by their power brought him forth;
when Mātariśvan churned him out, who was hidden in secret, for the sake of the sweet draught that has existed since ancient days.
When he is led forth from his father’s highest [abode], he rises wondrously upon the nourishing plants. When both parents hasten toward his birth, then the youngest became bright with fervor.
Then he entered the mothers, in whom the pure one, unhurt, has grown wide.
When he has climbed up after the former ones who were born together, he runs down among the newer, lower [sacrificial] grasses.
Then indeed they choose him as the Hotṛ-priest in the rites for reaching heaven; seeking to satisfy him, they strive toward him as if toward Bhaga.
When, praised by many, he goes with his wisdom and power among the gods and the assembly of mortals in every way, so that they may be nourished.
When he has spread out, the worshipful one, urged by the wind, like a whirling wheel, crooked and ageless, not fashioned by hands;
on the flight of that burning one, whose stride is black, who is born of light, the path extends through the mid-air. Like a chariot made by craftsmen, he speeds toward heaven with his ruddy limbs.
Then, O Agni, your black steeds, the wise ones, rush forth at your impetuous onset like the birds of a hero.

For by you, O Agni, Varuṇa whose laws are firm, Mitra, and the bounteous Aryaman have been made strong. Since you were born, encompassing all things with your will as the felly encompasses the wheel, you have become all-pervading.
O Agni, youngest one, you bestow wealth and the assembly of gods upon the one who exerts himself and presses the soma.
As such, O young son of strength, we establish you anew as our leader; like Bhaga, we fashion you, the possessor of great jewels, for our prayers.
Like a treasure of light, like the household lord, like Bhaga, and like Dakṣa, you have filled us with enduring strength.
He who, like reins, controls both worlds at their birth, the one of excellent wisdom who proclaims the praise of the gods according to the *ṛta*.
And may the radiant Hotṛ, with swift horses and a shining chariot, hear us—may he, the delightful one, listen to our call.
May that unerring Agni lead us by the best paths toward desirable wealth, prosperity, and greater well-being.
Agni has been praised with powerful hymns, bestowing further sovereignty for the sake of imperial rule.
May those wealthy patrons and we ourselves spread forth like the sun dispelling the mist.
O Agni, being kindled, bring the gods today to the one who holds the ladle.
Spin out the ancient thread for the donor who has pressed the Soma. O Tanūnapāt, measure out the oblation rich in ghee and honey for the inspired singer like me, who exerts himself as a donor.
Pure, purifying, and wonderful, he sprinkles the sacrifice with honey.
Narāśaṃsa, the god worthy of worship among the gods, thrice from heaven— O Agni, being invoked, bring here the bright and beloved Indra.
For this prayer of mine, O fair-tongued one, is directed toward you.
Spreading the sacrificial grass, with ladles extended, at the well-ordered sacrifice,
I prepare for Indra a wide-spreading shelter, most spacious for the gods.

May the great doors, which increase the cosmic order (*ṛta*), open wide for the gods to pass through— purifying, much-desired, divine, and unceasing. May Night and Dawn, the two well-adorned ones, being praised as they draw near, come together.
May the two great mothers who follow the *ṛta*, the two Hotṛ-priests, the divine seers with pleasant tongues who sing praises, sit upon the sacrificial grass with favor;
may they today perform for us this successful sacrifice that reaches the heavens.
Pure, the Hotrā offering is entrusted to the gods; Bhāratī among the Maruts;
may Iḷā, Sarasvatī, and Mahī sit upon the sacrificial grass, they who are worthy of worship.
Grant us that which is abundant, wondrous, rich in boons, and manifold in itself.
May Tvaṣṭṛ release [the sacrificial food] for nourishment and for wealth, being well-disposed toward our kinship.
Releasing [the offering] by yourself, O Vanaspati, sacrifice to the gods. For Agni, the wise god among the gods, prepares the oblations well.
To Vāyu, accompanied by Pūṣan, by the Maruts, and by all the gods;
to Indra, who is moved by the Gāyatrī, prepare the oblation with the cry of *svāhā*.
Come hither, O Agni, to the offerings consecrated with *svāhā*, to enjoy the oblations.
O Indra, come; hear our call. They invoke you at the sacrifice.
I bring forth a most powerful, newest prayer to Agni, a thought of speech for the Son of Strength.
He who is the dear grandson of the waters, the Hotṛ-priest who sits upon the earth in due season together with the Vasus.
Being born in the highest heaven, Agni became manifest to Mātariśvan. By the power and the greatness of him as he was being kindled, his radiance caused both Heaven and Earth to shine forth.
His flames are fierce and ageless; the beams of him who is beautiful to behold, whose face is fair, and whose splendor is bright, are lovely to see.
Those whose power is light, like rushing rivers, O Agni, tremble—unfailing and ageless ones.
Him, the all-knowing, whom the Bhr̥gus have established at the navel of the earth by the greatness of the world;
that Agni, do thou urge on with songs in your own home, he who alone rules over wealth like Varuṇa.

He who cannot be restrained like the roar of the Maruts, like an army let loose, or like a celestial thunderbolt—Agni eats with his sharpened jaws; he devours and overcomes the forests as a warrior overcomes his enemies.
Will Agni, the hero, grant us wealth for our hymn? Will he, together with the Vasus, fulfill our desire?
May he, the impeller, surely speed our prayers toward the attainment [of wealth]; him whose face is radiant, I praise with this most recent hymn.

To you, Agni—whose face is anointed with clarity, who sits at the yoke-pole of the Cosmic Order (ṛta), and whom they honor like Mitra when kindled—they approach. Kindling him, the unaging one, shining brightly in the assemblies, may he lift up our prayer toward the light-colored [dawn].
O Agni, with your unfailing, auspicious, and powerful guardians, protect us.
O Desired One, with those who are undeceived, undaunted, and unblinking, guard our offspring on every side.
The Hotṛ-priest goes forth according to his law by means of his creative power, holding aloft the pure-hued prayer.
He strides toward the ladles that turn to the right, which first kiss his primary abode.

The milking-streams of *ṛta* have lowed toward him, encompassed within the womb, at the seat of the god. When he dwelt distributed in the lap of the waters, then he sucked the *svadhā*-offerings by which he moves.
Desiring to win, those two of equal age strive together for that same wondrous form, each seeking their common goal with one another.
Then, like Bhaga, he is to be invoked by us; like a charioteer, he has gathered the reins.
The two Yamas, of equal age, serve him together—twins dwelling in a common womb and sharing a single abode.
By day as by night, the gray-haired one was born young; ageless, he traverses many human generations.
The ten fingers, our prayers, urge him on; we mortals invoke the god for protection.
From the dry land down the slope he speeds; with those who come toward him, he has established new paths.
For you, O Agni, rule over the celestial realm; you are the master of the earthly realm by your own power, like a herdsman.
These two great, golden, shimmering, and moving ones, adorned with splendor, have spread out upon the sacrificial grass for you.
O Agni, joyful one, self-sustained, born of Truth, and of noble will, take pleasure in and welcome this word!
You who are all-encompassing, beautiful to behold, and delightful to look upon, like a dwelling-place filled with food.

Ask him; he has gone there; he knows it. He, the wise one, is led forward; he indeed is led forward. In him are the instructions, in him are the desires; he is the lord of strength, of powerful vigor.
They ask him; he does not ask them back, for the wise one has grasped it with his own mind.
He does not forget the first word nor the later one; he follows his own will, undeluded. To him alone go the ladles and the swift mares; he alone shall hear all my words.
The one who sends forth many, the conqueror, the accomplisher of sacrifice, the one of unbroken lineage—the infant has assumed his vigorous strength.
Having approached, he moves as he was united; as soon as born, he strode forth with his companions.
He touches the glowing one for joy and delight, when the longing ones come to him who stands firm.
Like a wild beast of the waters or a ranger of the forest, he has been laid upon this most excellent skin.
Agni, the wise one who knows the *ṛta* and is true, has proclaimed the ways to mortals.
I praise the three-headed, seven-rayed, perfect Agni in the lap of his parents.
Seated upon him as he moves, the firm one has filled all the luminous realms of heaven.
As a great bull, he has grown toward these two; undecaying and lofty, he stands with his support.
He plants his footsteps on the ridges of the wide earth; his ruddy flames lick the udder.
Moving toward their common calf, the two well-established cows wander in all directions;
measuring out their paths that are never obstructed, they bestow all perceptions upon the great [ocean]. The wise poets lead to its station, guarding with various hearts the one who does not age.
Desiring to win, they looked all around at the river; Sūrya became manifest to the men.
Worthy to be beheld, born among the race-courses, he is to be invoked for the great and the small for their life.
Since he, the bounteous one visible to all, has appeared in many places for these embryos, the Sun.
How, O Agni, have the radiant ones offered to you, seeking strength with their swift offerings?
When the gods, bestowing both sons and grandsons, take delight in the chant of *ṛta*.
O youngest one, Lord of Self-power, take heed of this my most bountiful and presented speech.
One reviles, another praises; as your worshipper, O Agni, I laud your body.

Those guardians of yours, O Agni, who, seeing him, protected the blind son of Mamatā from misfortune— the All-Knowing One protected those doers of good deeds; though the enemies sought to deceive them, they did not succeed in deceiving them.

O Agni, whoever—being stingy, malevolent, and ungenerous—harms us with duplicity, may that heavy spell recoil upon him; may he destroy his own body with his evil words. Or even if some mortal, O powerful one, knowingly harms another mortal with duplicity.
From here, O Agni, being praised, protect the one who praises you; let no one be destined for misfortune on our account.

When Mātariśvan, having entered, churned him forth—the Hotṛ-priest who belongs to all waters and all gods, whom they have established among the human clans, bright as the sun, wondrous in form, and resplendent.
They have not deceived him who gives this prayer; Agni has delighted in my protection.
They have accepted all the works of this singer who brings forth praise. Him whom they have seized in his own eternal seat, the worshipful ones have established with their hymns of praise.
They lead him forward, grasping him in their desire, like swift horses of a chariot.
The wondrous one destroys many things with his jaws; radiant, he shines within the forest.
Then the wind blows after his flame, day after day, like an archer’s arrow shot from the bow.

Him whom neither enemies nor those seeking to harm can injure while he is yet in the womb—him, though blind and sightless, the harmful ones could not deceive by their observation; his own constant friends have protected him.
He, the lord of the house, seeks great wealth; he stands at the station of powerful treasure.
The pressing-stones have served him as he rushes forward;
he who is the bull of men, as it were, for both heaven and earth, whose flow is drunk by the living through his glories—
he who, having sped forth, has settled in his place of origin.
He who has shone upon the unassailable city,
the seer like a steed of the clouds, brilliant as the sun, possessing a hundredfold life-force;
he, the twice-born, shining brightly, has taken his stand over the three luminous realms and all the worlds.
The Hotṛ, most skilled in sacrifice, in the gathering place of the waters—
this is that Hotṛ who is twice-born and bestows all desirable things out of a desire for glory upon the mortal who, with noble intent, offers worship to him.
O Agni, as your devoted worshipper, I have spoken much to you, for you are indeed my friend.
Like the shelter of a great impeller, you are the refuge of the one who possesses wealth and is free from malice, even in the act of offering.
Never indeed [is there harm] for those who do not worship the gods.
That mortal, O inspired singer, is radiant, great, and most exalted in heaven.
May we, O Agni, be foremost among those who strive for you.
Him whom those seeking cattle, with skillful thought at the sacrifice, have generated among the waters like a friend— him, the beloved and worshipful one,

for whose sake the two worlds trembled at his splendor and his song, he protects our generation. For when that [sacrifice] of Purumīḷha, the possessor of Soma, was offered, those self-sustaining ones established it as they would friends.

Then find the will and the path for our praise; O powerful ones, hear the call of him who dwells by the waters. The peoples have adorned your birth from the two worlds, O powerful ones, to be proclaimed for the sake of great skill.
When you bring it for the sake of Truth and for the one who speeds along, you enjoy the sacrifice through the invocation of the Hotṛ-priest with vigor.
That people is indeed fortunate, O Asuras, which you two, possessors of truth, proclaim as the great Truth.

You two harness the creative power of the lofty heaven to set the waters in motion, like a bull to the yoke-pole. Here on earth, by your greatness, you two bring forth the desired object; the dustless, swift milch-cows sit in the dwelling-place.
They cry out toward the sun at its rising and at sunset, like swift birds at dawn.
The long-haired ones have sung in praise for the sake of cosmic order (*ṛta*), O Mitra and Varuṇa, where you two chant the path.
Release [the waters] by yourselves; cause our prayers to overflow. You two direct the inspired thought of the sage.

Whosoever, striving with sacrifices, offers gifts to you both—the sage who as Hotar-priest performs the sacrifice, accomplishing the prayer—unto him you two come; you enjoy the ritual, come toward our songs and our favor, seeking us.
You two, the first, anoint yourselves with sacrifices and with milk, O observers of Truth, at the stirrings of the mind.
They bring you songs with concentrated thought; with untroubled minds, you have attained wealth.
O Heroes, you bestow wealth as strength; through our prayers, you have attained wealth and greatness.
Neither the heavens with their days, nor the rivers, nor the Paṇis have attained your divinity or your bounty.
You two clothe yourselves in garments of milk; your thoughts are flawless, like continuous streams.
You have struck down all falsehoods; O Mitra and Varuṇa, you abide by the Eternal Law (ṛta). Not even one person among them understands this: the mantra proclaimed by the seer is true and formidable.
The fierce four-cornered one strikes the three-cornered; the revilers of the gods were the first to decay.
The footless one goes before those with feet; who, O Mitra and Varuṇa, understands this deed of yours?
The embryo bears the burden even as it comes from him; he fulfills the *ṛta* and overcomes the *anṛta*.
We behold him as he departs from here, the lover of maidens, who does not descend;
clad in wide-spreading, impenetrable garments, the beloved domain of Mitra and Varuṇa.
Born without a horse, without reins, the steed flies along, neighing loudly with his back uplifted.

The youthful ones have delighted in the unconscious Brahman, praising its foundation in Mitra and Varuṇa. May the milch-cows, favoring the son of Mamatā, cause him who loves the sacred word to swell with milk at this very udder.
Knowing the ways, let him beg for food; seeking to win her over, he shall preserve Aditi.

O Mitra and Varuṇa, O gods, may I turn you both toward the enjoyment of our oblation with reverence and for the sake of protection. May our prayer be victorious in battles; may we have divine rain that carries us safely across.
We worship you both, the great ones, being of one accord with oblations and salutations, O Mitra and Varuṇa.
O you who drip with ghee, when the Adhvaryus bring offerings for you with our prayers, like clarified butter;
O Mitra and Varuṇa, this well-fashioned hymn is offered to you as a presentation and an invocation.
When the Hotṛ priest anoints you in the assemblies, the patron, desiring to worship you, O powerful ones, seeks your favor.
The cow Aditi has swelled with milk for the sake of the Law (ṛta) and for the person who offers the oblation, O Mitra and Varuṇa.
When the human priest, serving you in the assembly and presenting the oblation, impels you both, he acts like a Hotar-priest.
Moreover, among the exhilarating clans, the cows and the divine waters have caused the soma-juice to swell for you.
And so may our ancient Lord of this [sacrifice] grant it; enjoy and drink of the milk of the ruddy cow.

Now, indeed, shall I proclaim the heroic deeds of Viṣṇu, who measured out the earthly realms and the regions of space; he who propped up the highest dwelling place, stroding across the three worlds, the wide-striding one.

For that heroic deed Viṣṇu is praised, like a terrifying wild beast, roaming far and dwelling in the mountains— he in whose three wide strides all living beings abide. Let this hymn go forth as strength to Viṣṇu, the dweller on the mountain, the wide-striding bull.
He who alone has measured out this long, extended common dwelling-place with three steps;
he whose three steps, full of honey, never-failing, enjoy themselves through their own inherent power;
and he who alone has supported the threefold earth and the sky, and all existing beings.
May I attain that beloved domain of his, where men devoted to the gods rejoice;
for there, in the highest step of Viṣṇu, the wide-striding one, is the kinsman and the fountain of honey. We desire to go to those dwellings of yours where the many-horned, restless cows abide.
Therein shines down the abundant, supreme station of that wide-striding bull.
Sing forth for the one who meditates with inspired thought upon the drinking of the soma-juice— for the great Hero and for Viṣṇu—
those two invincible ones who stand upon the ridges of the mountains like a horse on its proper course.
Such is the brilliant encounter of the two impetuous ones; O Indra and Viṣṇu, the drinker of the pressed juice protects you both.
You protect the swift bolt of Kr̥śānu when it is aimed against a mortal.
These [hymns] increase his great manly power; he brings down the two parents for the sake of seed and for enjoyment.

The son bestows upon his father a lower name, a higher one, and a third upon the luminous realm of heaven. We celebrate each of those manly deeds of this one who is seated, the protector, the harmless, the bountiful— He who, with three wide strides, has traversed the earthly realms for the sake of wide-striding life.
Beholding his two strides, the mortal who perceives the light hastens toward them; no one dares to approach his third stride, not even the winged birds as they fly through the air.
With four names at once, he has cast aside ninety [enemies], like a revolving wheel that sweeps away its spokes.
With a vast body, measuring himself out with the chanters, the youthful son of the two parents returns to the invocation.
Be gracious like a friend, O you who are anointed with clarity, whose splendor is far-reaching, who moves swiftly, and who are wide-extending.
Now, O Viṣṇu, even by the wise, your praise is to be honored; the sacrifice accompanied by oblations is to be performed for you.
He who offers worship to Viṣṇu— the ancient, the most recent, the ordainer, the one of noble kinship—
he who proclaims the great birth of this Great One shall indeed surpass even his peer in glory.
O singers, fulfill him by your very birth as the first-born, the germ of Cosmic Order (ṛta), just as you know him.
Knowing his very name, proclaim it! O Viṣṇu, we partake of your great benevolence.
King Varuṇa and the Aśvins attend to that will of his, the ordainer of the Maruts. Viṣṇu, possessing supreme skill and finding the day, supports the power and opens the stall for his friend.

Viṣṇu, the divine ordainer who is even more skilled than the skillful, has come to Indra for his companionship; he, the wise one dwelling in the three stations, has quickened the Ārya and granted the sacrificer a share in the portion of *ṛta*.
Agni has been awakened; the sun rises from the earth; the bright, radiant Dawn has shone forth with her great splendor.
The Aśvins have yoked their chariot to travel; the god Savitṛ has impelled the world apart.
O Aśvins, when you yoke your powerful chariot, sprinkle our dominion with ghee and honey. Strengthen our prayer in battles; may we share in the spoils in the contest for booty.
May the well-praised chariot of the Aśvins come hither—the three-wheeled, honey-bearing vehicle drawn by swift horses.
May the three-seated, bountiful lord of all prosperity bring welfare to our bipeds and quadrupeds.
O Aśvins, bring nourishment to us; sprinkle us with your honey-sweet whip.
May you extend our life; wipe away our sins; drive off our enemies; be our companions. You two place the embryo within moving creatures; you two are within all existing worlds.
O Ashvins, you two, the bulls, have caused Agni, the waters, and the lords of the forest to flow forth.
You two indeed are physicians with your medicines, and you are charioteers with your skill in driving.
Furthermore, O fierce ones, you bestow sovereign power upon that man who, possessing oblations, serves you with his whole mind.
O Vasus, Rudras, you of many insights, increasing [in strength], O bulls, grant us your favor in our desire for aid.
O wonder-workers, when Ucathya bestowed wealth upon you, and when you sped forth with your aids that are not solitary;

who may offer to you for this very favor of yours, O Vasus, when you bestow it through homage at the station of the Cow? Awaken for us wealthy inspirations, as you two move with a mind that fulfills every desire.
When your chariot, O ye two, was harnessed for the son of Tugra as a wide-sheltering vessel, it was established in the midst of the ocean, firm and strong.
May I come unto your protection for aid, like a hero to the battle with flying steeds.
May this hymn of praise preserve me from the son of Ucathya; let not these two winged ones exhaust me.
Let not the ten-fold piled wood consume me, when the bound man devours the earth before you both. The rivers, most motherly, did not swallow me up, though the Dāsas had cast me in tightly bound.
When Traitana hewed his head, the Dāsa himself gnawed his own breast and shoulders.
Dīrghatamas, son of Mamatā, having grown old in the tenth decade of life,
becomes the Brahman-priest and charioteer for those who strive toward the goal of the waters.
I praise with sacrifices the two great ones, Heaven and Earth, who increase the cosmic order (*ṛta*) and are wise in the assemblies.
Those who, with the gods, are the sons of the gods, performing wondrous deeds, bestow desirable boons through such inspired thought.
And I meditate upon the mind of the guileless Father and the greatness of the Mother; that power is inherent in them.
Through their invocations, the two parents of noble seed have made the world wide for their offspring, granting immortality through their far-reaching blessings.
Those sons, skillful in their work and wondrous in their deeds, brought forth two great mothers for the primordial perception.
By the law of all that is stationary and all that moves, you guard the station of the son who is free from duplicity.
Those wise ones, possessed of creative power, measured out the twin sisters of common origin, the paired ones dwelling in the same abode.

The wise poets, brilliantly shining, weave a new thread after a new one within the sky and the ocean. We meditate today upon that most excellent gift of Savitṛ at the impulse of the god. O Heaven and Earth, with benevolent intent, bestow upon us wealth abounding in treasures and consisting of hundreds.
For they, Heaven and Earth, are the source of all prosperity, observers of cosmic order (*ṛta*), and the wise sustainers of the realm.
Between these two well-born goddesses, the divine, radiant Sun moves according to the eternal law.
Far-extending, mighty, and inexhaustible, the Father and the Mother protect all living beings.
The two worlds, most bold and beautiful, were clothed by the Father with their various forms.
He, the wise son of the two parents, the bearer of the sacrifice, purifies the worlds through his creative power (*māyā*), possessing the means of purification.
Day by day, he milks the dappled cow and the bull of noble seed; his milk is ever bright.

O gods, he is the most skillful of craftsmen who brought forth the two worlds, the benefactors of all; he who, through his excellent wisdom, measured out the two regions with unaging supports and joined them together in song.
O Heaven and Earth, being praised by us, you two great ones shall bestow upon us great fame and lofty sovereign power.
RV 1.160.5: With that [power] by which we may always extend ourselves over the peoples, grant us praiseworthy strength.

RV 1.161.1: What has the best one come to us? What has the youngest come? For what mission is he going? When did we say it? RV 1.161.2: We have not reviled the cup which is of noble lineage; O Agni, brother, we have indeed praised the excellence of the wooden vessel.

"Make one chalice into four; that is what the gods told you, and for that reason I have come to you. "O sons of Sudhanvan, if you will do exactly this, you shall become worthy of sacrifice together with the gods.
"When you spoke to Agni the messenger, you said: 'A horse must be fashioned, and a chariot must also be made here.'"
"A cow must be made, two youths must be made"—these were the tasks you set for yourselves, O brothers; we have come to you after having accomplished them.
Having performed those deeds, O Ṛbhus, you asked: "Where has he gone, that messenger who came to us?
When Tvaṣṭṛ had announced that the four cups had been fashioned, he then hid himself among the divine wives.
"Let us slay them," so said Tvaṣṭṛ, "those who have reviled the cup from which the gods drink.

They assume other names at the pressed juice; with names other than their own, the maiden has preserved them. Indra yoked his two bay horses, the Aśvins [yoked] their chariot, and Bṛhaspati brought the one of all forms.
Ṛbhu, Vibhvan, and Vāja went to the gods; you, skillful-handed ones, obtained your share of the sacrifice.

By means of your inspired thoughts, you brought forth the cow from the hide; those who were aging, you made young again. O sons of Sudhanvan, you fashioned horse after horse; having yoked the chariot, you approached the gods.
"Drink this water," you said; "or rather, drink this rinsing-water of the *muñja* grass. "O sons of Sudhanvan, if you do not find pleasure in that, then rejoice at the third libation.
One said, "Water is most abundant"; another said, "Fire is most abundant."
One spoke out against many who were striking [the victim]: "Speak the truth; fashion the cups!
One drives the lame cow down to the water; one carves the meat brought on the carving-board. One carries away the dung until sunset. What indeed did the two parents do for their sons?
On the heights you provided grass for him, and in the valleys, O men, you performed your skillful work with water.

Since you were in the house of Agohya, O Ṛbhus, that which was there today you do not follow after here. When you crept around the worlds with eyes closed, where indeed did those two venerable fathers dwell?
He who seized your foreleg was cursed; he who spoke against you, you spoke back to him.
O Ṛbhus, while you were sleeping, you asked this of Agohya: "Who has awakened us here?
The goat declared the dog to be the awakener; today, after a full year, this world has been revealed.
By day the Maruts go; Agni goes upon the earth; this Vāta goes through the mid-air.
Varuṇa goes with the waters and the oceans, seeking you, O sons of strength.
May Mitra, Varuṇa, Aryaman, Āyu, Indra, Ṛbhukṣan, and the Maruts not overlook us.
When we shall proclaim in the assembly the heroic deeds of the prize-winning steed, born of the gods;
when they lead by the mouth the captured joy of him who is covered with a brilliant robe and wealth;
then the well-leaping, lowing, all-shaped one goes to the beloved path of Indra and Pūṣan.
This goat, the portion for Pūṣan, belonging to all the gods, is led before the vigorous horse. When Tvaṣṭṛ quickens this beloved sacrificial cake together with the horse for the sake of high renown,
then the men lead the horse three times around the oblation that is fit for the gods and follows the seasons along the path to the deities.
Here the goat, the first portion of Pūṣan, goes forth, announcing the sacrifice to the gods. The Hotṛ, the Adhvaryu, the Āvayāj, the kindler of Agni, the presser of the stones, and the wise reciter—
fill the bellies with this well-prepared, well-offered sacrifice.
Those who hew the sacrificial posts, those who carry the posts, and those who carve the crest-ring for the horse’s post;
and those who prepare the cooking-vessel for the steed—may their approval further us.
The smooth-backed steed has come near; my prayer has been offered toward the regions of the gods.
The wise seers rejoice after him; we have made him a close kinsman in the prosperity of the gods.

Whatever tethering strap of the prize-winning steed, whatever head-halter or cord belongs to him, or whatever grass has been placed in his mouth as fodder—all these things of yours shall remain with the gods.
Whatever of the horse’s raw flesh the fly has eaten, or whatever remains smeared on the sacrificial post or the axe;
whatever is on the hands of the immolator or on his nails—all that of yours shall belong to the gods.
Whatever undigested contents of the belly escape, and whatever odor there is of the raw flesh—[all that belongs to the gods].

Let the skilled immolators prepare that; let them cook the sacrificial victim until it is thoroughly roasted. Whatever from your limb, as it is being cooked by fire while you are fixed upon the spit, drips down—let that not fall upon the earth nor upon the grass; let it be offered to the gods who desire it.

Those who look upon the cooked sacrificial horse, those who say, "It is fragrant; take it out," and those who wait for a portion of the flesh of the steed—may their approval also further us. The probe used for the cauldron in which the meat is cooked, the vessels for pouring the broth, and the ladles...
The warm coverings, the cooking pots, the hooks, and the slaughter-stakes attend upon the horse. His stepping-place, his resting-place, his turning-place, and the tethering-rope of the steed—
whatever he has drunk and whatever fodder he has eaten— all these of yours shall be among the gods.

Let not the smoke-scented fire crackle against you, nor let the glowing cauldron burst as it cooks. The gods accept that horse which has been sacrificed, offered, approved, and consecrated with the cry of *vaṣaṭ*.
The garment they spread for the horse, the upper covering, and the pieces of gold that are placed for him—
The halter, the foot-rope, and the dear trappings they bring for the steed among the gods.
Whatever pain was caused to you while being mounted— by the greatness of the rider, or by the heel, or by the whip—
I soothe all those [pains] of yours with a sacred prayer (*brahman*), as one offers oblations with a ladle at the sacrifices.
The axe meets the thirty-four ribs of the horse, the steed of the Friend of the Gods. Make its limbs flawless; fashion them with skill, joint by joint, proclaiming it as you dissect it.
There is one dissector of Tvaṣṭṛ’s horse, and there are two who guide him, according to the sacred law.
Those of your limbs which I prepare in due order, those very portions I offer as balls of meat into the fire.
Let not your dear soul burn you as you depart; let not the axe linger upon your body.
Let not the greedy disemboweler, overstepping his mark, pierce through your limbs haphazardly with the knife.
Truly, you do not die here, nor are you harmed; you go to the gods by easy paths.
Your two bay steeds and the two spotted mares have been yoked; the prize-winning steed has taken its place at the pole of the donkey.
May this prize-winning steed grant us abundance of cattle and fine horses, heroic sons, and all-sustaining wealth.
May Aditi grant us freedom from sin; may the horse, accompanied by the oblation, win sovereign power for us.
When you first neighed at birth, rising from the ocean or from the watery depths—with the wings of a falcon and the forelegs of an antelope—great was your wondrous birth, O steed worthy of praise.
Yama gave him; Trita harnessed him; Indra was the first to mount him.
The Gandharva grasped his reins; O Vasus, you fashioned the horse from the sun. You are Yama, O steed; you are Āditya; you are Trita by your secret ordinance.
You are separated from Soma by a measure; they say you have three bonds in heaven. They say you have three bonds in heaven, three in the waters, and three within the ocean.
And Varuṇa seems to me to be entangled, where they say is your highest place of birth.
O Steed, here are your grooming brushes; here are the places where you set down your hooves as you win the prize.
Here I beheld your auspicious reins, which are the guardians that protect the laws of Truth (*ṛta*).
With my mind I have recognized your very self, the bird flying through the sky from heaven.
I beheld thy head hastening along easy paths, dustless and winged.
There I saw thy most excellent form, striving to win the nourishment at the cow’s station. When the mortal has yielded to thy enjoyment, then, as the greatest devourer, thou hast awakened the plants.
After you, O steed, comes the chariot; after you, the young bridegroom; after you, the cattle; after you, the fortune of maidens.
After you, the throngs have sought your friendship; the gods have measured out your heroic power.
Golden-horned, with iron hooves, swift as thought—Indra was inferior to him.

The gods indeed came to eat the oblation of him who was the first to mount the courser. With their limbs at the ends and their slender waists, the divine coursers, like heroes, rush together. Like swans they draw up in rows when the horses have reached the celestial course.
Your body, O Forest-Strider, is winged; your mind is swift-gliding like the wind.
Your horns are established in many places; they move flickeringly within the forests.
The prize-winning steed has come near to the place of slaughter, meditating with a mind directed toward the gods.
The Unborn One is led in front; his kinship follows behind him as the sages move along with their songs.
He has approached the highest dwelling place, turning hither toward father and mother. Today he shall go to the gods as one most welcome; then he bestows desirable boons upon the donor.
Of this lovely, grey-haired Hotṛ-priest, there is a middle brother who is voracious;
his third brother has ghee upon his back. Here I beheld the Lord of the People, who has seven sons.
Seven harness the chariot that has but one wheel; a single horse draws it, bearing seven names.
The wheel with three naves, undecaying and irresistible, upon which all these worlds rest. Upon this seven-wheeled chariot stand the seven; seven horses draw it.
Seven sisters sing together toward it, where the seven names of the cows are deposited.
Who has seen him being born for the first time, when the boneless one supports that which possesses bones?
Where indeed is the life-force and the blood of the earth? Who has approached the wise man to ask this?
Being simple-minded and lacking understanding in my mind, I ask about these hidden footsteps of the gods.
Upon the young calf, the seven threads have been stretched out for the sake of weaving;
I, the unknowing, ask the knowing sages here for the sake of knowledge, not being one who knows. What indeed is that One, in the form of the Unborn, who has propped apart these six worlds?
Let him who truly knows this declare here the hidden station of this lovely bird.
From its head the cows milk forth the milk; clothed in their covering, they have drunk the water with their feet.
In the beginning, the Mother shared her portion with the Father according to the *ṛta*; for she united with him through meditation and mind.
She, loathsome with the essence of the embryo, was pierced; then those full of reverence approached her with their prayer.
The Mother was yoked to the pole of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*); the embryo stood within the enclosures.
The calf lowed as it beheld the cow of all forms in the three distances.

Bearing three mothers and three fathers, he stands alone, erect; they do not weary him. Upon the back of that sky, they deliberate in speech that knows all things and stirs all. That twelve-spoked wheel of *ṛta* revolves around the heavens; it does not decay.
RV 1.164.11: O Agni, here the sons have stood in pairs—seven hundred and twenty.
RV 1.164.12: They say that the Father has five feet and twelve forms; he who abounds in moisture dwells in the further half of heaven.
And these others say that the far-seeing one is fixed upon the lower seven-wheeled, six-spoked [chariot].
Upon the five-spoked wheel that revolves, all living beings stand.

Its axle, though bearing a heavy burden, does not grow hot; its nave, from of old, does not wear away. The wheel with its rim, ageless, rolls on; ten yoked together draw it upon the outstretched [nave].
The eye of the Sun pervades the encompassed mid-world; in it all beings are established.
Of those born together, they call the seventh one "the single-born"; the six are called "twins," the seers, and "born of the gods.
Their desired abodes are ordained according to their stations; they tremble before the Sustainer, transformed according to their forms.

They who are women, these the men call; he who has eyes sees them, yet the blind man does not perceive them. The son who is a seer has understood them; he who knows them shall become the father of his father.
Beneath the higher and above the lower, the cow has risen up, bearing her calf with her foot.
Whither has she gone? To which side has she departed? Where does she bring forth offspring, for she is not within the herd?

He who, by means of that which is below, knows the Father of this [world], and he who, by means of that which is above, knows the one beyond—being a seer, who here can declare from whence divine mind was born?
Those who go hitherward they call "going away," and those who go away they call "coming hither.
O Indra and Soma, those things which you two have fashioned are carried like yoked horses through the mid-air. Two birds of beautiful plumage, inseparable companions, embrace the same tree.
Of these two, one eats the sweet fruit of the fig tree, while the other looks on without eating.
Where those with beautiful wings, never blinking, sing together toward their share of immortality,
there the wise guardian of the entire world has entered me, the simple-minded.

On that tree where all the fair-winged ones, eaters of honey, settle and bring forth their young—of that tree they say the fruit at the top is sweet; he does not reach it who does not know his father.
When the *gāyatra* is placed upon the *gāyatra*, or when they fashioned the *traiṣṭubha* from the *traiṣṭubha*...
Or whatever moving thing has been placed upon the earth—those who know that have attained immortality.

With the *gāyatrī* he measures out the hymn (*arka*), with the hymn the *sāman*, and with the *triṣṭubh* the recitation (*vāka*). With the recitation he measures out the recitation; by means of the two-footed and four-footed syllable, they measure out the seven voices.

With the *jagatī* he caused the Sindhu to swell; with the *rathantara* he beheld the sun. They say there are three kindling-sticks for the *gāyatrī*; by its greatness it has surpassed [them] in majesty.
I call hither this well-milking cow; may the skillful milker milk her.
May Savitṛ impel for us the most excellent impulse; the Gharma has been heated—this indeed I shall proclaim.

Uttering the sound *hiṅ*, the mistress of treasures, seeking her calf with her mind, has approached. May she, the inviolable cow, yield milk for the Aśvins; may she increase for our great good fortune.
The cow lowed after her blinking calf; she made her head to be measured out.
Licking the warm milk with longing, she utters her cry and yields her milk with her streams.
This is he who bellows, by whom the cow is covered; she utters her cry, resting upon the dark place.
By her thoughts she has indeed brought the mortal down; becoming lightning, she has stripped away her covering.
The swift-moving one has reached the living, the trembling one, the firm one in the midst of the dwellings.
The living moves by means of the offerings of the dead; the immortal shares a common womb with the mortal.
I beheld the Herdsman, never resting, moving hither and thither along his paths.
Clothing himself in converging and diverging rays, he revolves repeatedly within the worlds.
He who made him knows nothing of him; he who saw him is far removed from him.
Enveloped within his mother’s womb, he who possesses many offspring has entered into destruction. Heaven is my father, my progenitor; here is my navel. This great earth is my kin, my mother.
Between the two upturned bowls is the womb; there the father placed the embryo of his daughter.
I ask you about the furthest limit of the earth; I ask where the navel of the world is.
I ask you about the seed of the stallion; I ask about the highest heaven of speech.
This altar is the furthest limit of the earth; this sacrifice is the navel of the world.
This Soma is the seed of the bull, the horse; this is the Brahman, the highest heaven of speech.
Seven half-germs, the seed of the world, stand by the command of Viṣṇu in the supporting law.
They, through their insights and their mind, being wise, as all-encompassing masters, encompass everything on every side.
I do not discern what this is that I am; hidden and girded with the mind, I move. When the first-born of *ṛta* come to me, then I attain a share of this speech.
Held by its own inherent power, the immortal goes forth from the waters, sharing a common womb with the mortal.
Those two, eternal and moving in opposite directions, pass along; they have perceived one, but they have not perceived the other.
In the syllable of the *ṛc*, in the highest heaven, upon which all the gods have settled— he who does not know that, what will he do with the *ṛc*? But those who know it, they sit together here.
O blessed one, may you have abundant good pasture; and may we also be blessed. Eat grass, O inviolable one, at all times; drink pure water as you wander.
The buffalo has lowed, fashioning the waters; she is one-footed, two-footed, and four-footed.
She has become eight-footed, nine-footed, possessing a thousand syllables in the highest heaven.
From her the oceans flow forth; by that the four quarters of space live.
Thence flows the imperishable syllable; upon that everything lives.
From afar I beheld the smoke, consisting of power, spreading far and wide, beyond this lower world.
The heroes cooked the speckled bull; those were the first ordinances.
Three long-haired ones appear in due season; one of them shears his hair within the year.
One beholds all things through his powers; the flash of the One is seen in his form.
Speech has been measured out in four quarters; those Brahmins who are wise know them.
Three, hidden in secret, do not stir; of speech, mortals speak only the fourth quarter.
They call him Indra, Mitra, Varuṇa, and Agni; and he is the divine, fair-winged Garuḍa.
That which is one, the sages call by many names: they speak of it as Agni, Yama, and Mātariśvan.
The dark path, the golden-winged birds, clothed in water, fly up toward heaven.
They have returned from the seat of Cosmic Order; since then, the earth has been sprinkled with clarified butter.
Twelve are its spokes, one its wheel, and three its naves—who indeed has understood that?
Upon it are fixed together thirty nails, and sixty that are unshakable.
That breast of yours which is inexhaustible, which is a source of bliss, by which you nourish all desirable things;
that which bestows jewels, finds wealth, and grants good gifts—O Sarasvatī, bring that here for us to suck.
By means of sacrifice the gods sacrificed to the sacrifice; those were the first established ordinances.
These great ones have attained the firmament, where the ancient Sādhyas, the gods, abide.
This same water rises up and falls down day after day; Parjanya quickens the earth, and the fires quicken the heavens.
The divine, well-winged, great bird, the offspring of the waters, the most beautiful among the plants;
him who satisfies us from all sides with rains, Sarasvant, I invoke for protection.
With what splendor have the Maruts, of equal age and common dwelling, united together?

With what thought have they come from where? These bulls roar their strength, desiring wealth. Whose prayers have the youths accepted? Who has turned the Maruts toward his sacrifice? Like hawks gliding through the mid-air, by what great spirit may we cause them to pause?

RV 1.165.3: From where do you come, O Indra, you who are mighty? Why, O Lord of the Good, do you go alone? What is it that you ask thus of us as you approach with the radiant ones? Tell us that, O Lord of the Bay Horses, which is yours among us.
RV 1.165.4: My sacred prayers and my thoughts [are here]; the pressed juices are auspicious; my strength stirs, and the pressing-stone is set forth for me.
They pray for him; they welcome the hymn with longing. These two bay steeds carry him toward us.

From there, we, yoking these well-matched companions and adorning our bodies with our own powers, now harness them according to our greatness. For you, O Indra, have come to be according to our self-power (*svadhā*).
RV_01.165.06.1 Where was that self-power of yours, O Maruts, when you left me alone in the slaying of Ahi?
RV_01.165.06.2 For I am indeed fierce, powerful, and mighty; I have bent down every enemy with my weapons.
RV_01.165.07.1 You have achieved much with us as your allies, O Bull, through our shared manly deeds.
RV_01.165.07.2: For we two, O most powerful Indra and Maruts, shall indeed accomplish many things through our will, whatever we may desire.
RV_01.165.08.1: With my own power and with my fury, O Maruts, I slew Vṛtra; I became mighty. RV_01.165.08.2:
I, with the thunderbolt in my arm, have made these all-glittering waters flow easily for Manu.
O Maghavan, you are unsurpassed; indeed, no one among the gods is known to be your equal.

Neither one being born nor one already born can attain that which you shall do, O Increaser—do it now! Though I am alone, my strength is manifold; whatever I, daringly, shall accomplish through my inspired thought, let it be done.
For I, O Maruts, am known as the fierce one; Indra alone is the lord of those things which I set in motion.
O Maruts, you rejoiced here in my hymn of praise, since you, O heroes, have fashioned for me a sacred prayer worthy of renown.
For Indra, the bull, the noble warrior—for me, your friend—O friends, you have done this for your own bodies with your very selves.
Thus indeed these Maruts, shining toward me, free from blemish, bestowing glory upon me—having beheld you, O moon-colored ones, you have pleased me; do so even now!
Who among you here, O Maruts, has magnified you? Come forward, O friends, toward your friends!
May they, the wondrous ones, cause my prayers to be heard; be mindful of these my true words.
Since the wisdom of Mānya has brought us here, as a poet brings honor for his service, O Maruts, turn hither quickly toward the inspired singer; let the chanter recite these sacred hymns for you.

This hymn is for you, O Maruts; this song is from Māndārya, the son of Māna, the singer. May it bring offspring for our own bodies; may we find strengthening food and a community that bestows life-sustaining gifts. Now let us proclaim the former greatness of that impetuous host, of the bull whose banner is light.
Like kindling on your march, O Maruts, you roar loudly; like warriors in battle, O Śakras, display your powers!
Carrying sweetness like a son to his own parents, they play their playful games, impetuous in the assemblies.
The Rudras reach the worshipper with their protection; being self-strong, they do not neglect the one who offers oblations.
To him for whom the immortal helpers have granted abundance of wealth because he has honored them with oblation—
to him the Maruts, bringing delight, sprinkle many regions with milk like well-disposed friends.
They who have clothed themselves in the regions with their powers— their swift-moving steeds have rushed forward.
All beings tremble; even the dwellings shake at your brilliant onset when your spears are brandished.

When you of heroic might cause the mountains to roar with your flashing course, or when you shake the very back of heaven, every lord of the forest fears at your coming, and the plants spring forward as if they were chariot-drivers.
O fierce Maruts, you whose hosts are unharmed, fulfill our desire with your benevolence.
Wherever your lightning, with its crackling teeth, bites, it releases the cattle with a force as if they were well-placed.
They who grant firm support, whose gifts are inexhaustible, who do not withhold their bounty, and who are well-praised at the assemblies.
They sing their song for the drinking of the exhilarating juice; they know the first heroic deeds of the Mighty One.
O Maruts, protect with hundred-gated forts that man from injury and evil whom you have favored.
O fierce, powerful, and exuberant ones, preserve the person from reproach in the prosperity of his offspring.

All auspicious things are upon your chariots, O Maruts; as if in rivalry with one another, your powers are placed there. Rings are upon your shoulders for the long journeys; your axle revolves between the two wheels. Many auspicious things are in your manly arms; upon your chests are golden ornaments, impetuous and glittering.
Upon their shoulders are these [ornaments], and upon their fellies are sharp razors; like birds spreading their wings, they have displayed their splendors.

Great by greatness, pervasive in their manifestations, visible from afar like the heavens with their stars—joyful, sweet-tongued, and resonant with their mouths, the Maruts surround Indra, chanting their hymns of praise.
O well-born Maruts, that is your greatness; long is your bounty, like the ordinance of Aditi.
Even Indra does not, by his abandonment, frustrate that [bounty] for the man of good deeds to whom you have been gracious.
O Maruts, that kinship of yours which you, the immortals, have extended widely in former ages—[for that we pray].
