Through this prayer, you have granted hearing to Manu; together with their wondrous deeds, the heroes have made themselves known. O swift Maruts, may we flourish through this your abundant wealth, by which we may extend far in the assembly of men. Through these sacrifices, may I attain that desired goal.
This hymn for you...
A thousand are your aids, O Indra; a thousand are the most praiseworthy refreshments, O Lord of the Bay Steeds.
May a thousand riches come to us for our delight; may thousandfold strengths approach us.
May the Maruts come toward us with their aids—those of great power, dwelling in the lofty heavens, and possessed of wondrous skill.
And when their teams of horses, even the most distant, hasten forth upon the far shore of the ocean;
they in whom the well-placed, ghee-anointed ladle clings like a spear with a golden hilt.

Moving in secret like a woman among men, Vāk (Speech) gathers together like one who presides over an assembly or a sacrificial rite. The radiant, tireless Maruts have mingled with the youthful [waters] as if they were common property.
The terrible gods did not push away heaven and earth; rather, they accepted the strengthening [oblation] for friendship.
If she, the divine one, should find pleasure in accompanying us, she who has loosened her locks, whose mind is set on manly deeds, may she come to the two worlds, Rodasī.
Like Sūryā, she has mounted the chariot of her worshipper; with her brilliant countenance, she comes like the onset of the clouds.
The young men have established the young woman, who blinks for beauty and is ever-present at the assemblies.
When the *arka*-singer, possessing oblations, sings a song for you, O Maruts, having pressed the Soma and offering his service;
I proclaim that which is to be proclaimed— the true greatness of these Maruts— when they,
with their bull-like minds and full of self-confidence, carry along even firm and fortunate wives.
Mitra and Varuṇa protect [us] from blame; Aryaman restrains those who are unworthy of praise.
Even the immovable and firm things are shaken; the Maruts, who bestow boons, have grown strong.
Indeed, O Maruts, no one among us has reached the limit of your power, even from afar, O mighty ones.
They, having increased with bold power, have boldly surrounded their enemies like a wave.
May we today be the dearest to Indra, and may we call upon him tomorrow in the assembly.
May we be so in the past; may he favor us day after day, and may Ṛbhukṣan, O heroes, grant this to us.
This is your hymn... [RV 1.167.11.1] At every sacrifice, you are alike in your swift conquest; you accept prayer after prayer as those who favor the gods.
May I turn you hither with well-fashioned hymns for the sake of great prosperity and for protection from heaven and earth. [RV 1.168.01.1–02]
Like self-born plants, they who are self-strong have been born toward nourishment and light, the shakers;

like thousandfold waves of the waters, they are to be praised with the mouth like bulls or stallions. Like pressed Soma drops, they whose stalks are satiated, having been drunk into the hearts, sit like those who offer service.
Upon their shoulders they bear [the spears] like hanging creepers; in their hands they hold the *khādi* and the *cakṛti*.

Their self-yoked [steeds] have come down from heaven at will; O immortals, urge yourselves on with the whip! Free from dust, born of themselves, the Maruts with glittering spears have cast down even the firm things.
O Maruts, who among you shakes [the world] within, like lightning with spears, by his own power, as if with the tongue of his jaws?
They shake the desert wastes like the onset of arrows; they have many commands, like the sun’s steed Etaśa on its daily course.
Where, O Maruts, is the furthest limit of this great expanse, and where its lowest depth, wherein you have come together?
When you cause that which was joined together to fall apart, as if it were unstable, you fly with the mountain, creating a shimmering ocean.
Your overwhelming assault is like a flood—mighty, radiant, dazzling, and crushing, O Maruts.
Blessed is your bounty, like the sacrificial fee of one who gives abundantly; wide-reaching, it crackles like the power of the Asuras.
The rivers roar back toward the tires [of their chariots] when they send forth their thunderous voice from the clouds. The lightnings smile down upon the earth when the Maruts sprinkle the ghee.
Pr̥śni brought forth for the great battle the brilliant host of the tireless Maruts.
Those Sapsaras gave birth to the vast one; from the beginning, they beheld the vigorous *svadhā*.
This is your hymn...
O Indra, you are indeed great, since you are the protector of these [beings], even from great abandonment.
O wise ordainer of the Maruts, being mindful, win for us their favors, for they are most dear to you.
These [Maruts], O Indra, have yoked themselves for all peoples, knowing how to ward off those who act against mortals.
The host of the Maruts, ever victorious, comes forth for the winning of light and the prize of the great battle.
Firmly fixed for us, O Indra, is that spear of yours; the Maruts impel their horse-like power without limit.
For even Agni, when kindled and blazing, bestows nourishing foods like waters upon an island. Do you then, O Indra, grant us that wealth as a gift with most powerful sacrificial fees.
And those hymns of yours which have been praised, O Vāyu—may they cause us to swell with the sweetness of honey and with strengths.
In you, O Indra, are riches most bountiful, leaders of every righteous man.
May those Maruts be gracious to us, they who of old were like gods seeking a path.
Go forth toward the bounteous men, O Indra; exert yourself in the great earthly dwelling.
And when their broad-based spears stand firm like women at a ford, displaying their manly prowess—then hear the thundering roar of these approaching Maruts, terrible and unremitting.
Those who with their protections strike down the mortal who attacks in battle, like debtors with their discharges;
O Indra, together with the Maruts, grant to the Mānas all people’s wealth, beginning with cattle.
Being praised by the gods, O God, may we find strengthening food and a community that bestows life-sustaining gifts.
There is nothing truly "now," nor is there anything for "tomorrow"; who knows that which is mysterious?
The mind of another is to be approached with caution, and even what has been learned may perish. Why, O Indra, do you seek to strike us down? The Maruts are your brothers.
Be well-disposed toward us with these; do not strike us in the encounter.
"What do you think, O brother Agastya, being our friend? For we know how your mind is; you do not wish to give to us."
Let them prepare the altar; let them kindle the fire in front.
There we two shall extend for you the sacrifice, the manifestation of immortality.
You, O Lord of Wealth, rule over riches; you, O Lord of friends, are the most generous among friends.
O Indra, converse with the Maruts; then consume the oblations in due season.
With this homage I come toward you; with this hymn I beg for the favor of the swift ones. O Maruts, bestowing gifts through your wisdom, lay aside your anger and unyoke your horses.

This hymn of yours, O Maruts, accompanied by reverence, fashioned by the heart and conceived by the mind, has been offered, O gods. Come hither, taking pleasure in it with your minds, for you are indeed the increasers of our homage.
May the Maruts, being praised, be gracious to us; and may the Maghavan, the most beneficent, being praised, grant us well-being.
May our beloved forests stand upright; O Maruts, may we conquer all days.
Trembling with fear of that powerful Indra, I flee from him, O Maruts. For you, the oblations were prepared and sharpened; we have now set them aside—be gracious to us!

By whom even the Mānasas were made mindful at the dawning of the eternal mornings through his power—may he, the bull, bestow glory upon us with the Maruts; may he, the fierce one, the steadfast giver of victory, be fierce with the fierce ones.
O Indra, protect the men from the more powerful; together with the Maruts, be one whose wrath is turned away.
May we, through those of excellent wisdom, be victorious and obtain nourishment—
O Vājas! May your journey be brilliant, O bounteous givers, brilliant with your aid,
O Maruts who shine like serpents!
Far away from you, O bounteous Maruts, let that rushing arrow go;
far away cast off the stone you hurl! O bounteous ones, spare the people of Tr̥ṇaskanda.
Raise us up that we may live!
Sing the *sāman* that is like the roar of the wind; let us chant with our hymn that which increases and is full of light.
The milch-cows, inviolable, are upon the sacred grass (*barhis*), as they seek to win the divine dwelling.
The roaring bull, with the sweating bulls as his oblations, like a wild beast, shall leap beyond the one who would devour him.
The exhilarated priest, the praised invoker, the worshipful youth, brings the pair forward.
May the Hotṛ-priest reach the measured seats as he goes; may he bear the germ of the earth through the autumns.
The horse neighs as he is led; the bull bellows; like a messenger between the two worlds, the voice moves.
Men seeking the gods bring these deeds and mighty exploits to him, for Indra, of wondrous luster, takes pleasure in them—he who stands upon his chariot, as easy to approach as the Nāsatyas.
Praise that Indra, who is indeed a warrior, who is the hero, the bounteous lord, who stands upon the chariot;
who, possessing the bull-strength, is a more formidable fighter even than those facing him, and the dispeller of even the most dense darkness.
Since he thus surpasses men in greatness, the two worlds, heaven and earth, are not even a girth for him.
Indra has encompassed the earth as if with a stronghold; self-sustaining, he supports the sky as if it were a canopy.
O Hero, in battles we seek to win over you, the protector of the virtuous and the foremost traveler.
With one accord, the people in their exhilaration delight Indra—the patron—just as they rejoice in the spoils of war.
For thus indeed are the libations a joy for you in the ocean, when the divine waters rejoice within them.
Every cow has become pleasing to you, even when you, through your inspired thought, visit the patrons and the people.
May we be well-favored by him, like those who possess good friends, through the praises of men, so that we may be victorious.
So that Indra may stand by our hymns of praise, like a swift one guiding his deeds and our recitations;
so that Indra with the thunderbolt in his hand may be on our side,
like those seeking Mitra among the leaders of men, well-guided, and like those seeking the center who serve with sacrifices.
For indeed, O Indra, no sacrifice, however it may falter or be approached with a wandering mind, ever fails you;
as one reaches home at a ford when thirsty, or as a long road brings the successful traveler, so do you come to us.
O Indra, let there be no conflict for us here among the gods, for you, O Mighty One, possess those who are yours.
Even the great song of the one who offers oblations praises the bounteous Maruts, whose youthful power is vast.
This hymn of praise, O Indra, is for you; through this, O Lord of Bay Steeds, find a path for us.
O God, turn toward us for our well-being; may we obtain food and progeny.
O Indra, King of kings, and you gods, protect us; O Asura, guard us as men!
You are the Lord of the righteous, our bounteous deliverer; you are the true one, the possessor of wealth, the giver of strength.
O Indra, you shattered the seven autumnal fortresses, the refuge of the Danus who spoke with insults.
O blameless one, you released the waters; you delivered Vṛtra over to the young Purukutsa.
O Indra, invoked by many, with those [allies] by whom the goat-like women were won for the hero, and heaven itself, you now [protect us].
Like a lion in his den, you, the tireless Tūrvayāṇa, have performed deeds of power for the protection of Agni and the dawn.
O Indra, may they remain for you in this same place for the praise of your greatness, O wielder of the thunderbolt.
When you released the waters and the cattle through battle, your two bay steeds stood firm; with boldness, you swept away the spoils of war.
O Indra, carry Kutsa, in whom you took delight—his two bay horses, swift as the wind, were harnessed by cords.
May the Sun’s wheel roll forward in the encounter; may he whose arm wields the thunderbolt advance against his rivals.

Indra, grown strong through his own power, O Lord of Bay Steeds, has struck down those who do not give, having slain the Mitrerus as they fled, while Aryaman looked on from the side of the righteous, as they were being shattered by you while carrying their offspring.
The sage has whispered, O Indra, for the winning of the sun; he has made the earth a cushion for the Dāsa.
Maghavan has fashioned three wonderful gifts; he has cast Kuyavāc into a pit of misfortune.
These ancient deeds of yours, O Indra, have become new again; you have brought many clouds down for the sake of the hero’s release.
He shattered the godless fortresses as if they were earthen mounds; he struck down the weapon of the godless oppressor who offered no homage.
O Indra, you, the shaker, set in motion the waters that shake with force, like flowing rivers.
When you, O hero, carried across the ocean, you brought Turvaśa and Yadu safely to the further shore.
O Indra, may you always be ours—the most protective of men, the guardian of heroes. As such, grant us victory over all our adversaries.
O Lord of the Bay Steeds, let the exhilarating, intoxicating draught be drunk by you, like the great contents of a vessel.
O Bull, for you, the bull, the Soma-drop is vigorous, a prize-winner, most effective at winning thousands.
May the exhilarating, bull-like, and excellent intoxicant come to us—
victorious, Indra-like, all-gaining, immortal, and a conqueror in battle.
For you, O hero, are the winner; you urge on the chariot of man. As a conqueror, you have stolen away the lawless Dasyu with your flame, like a vessel [filled] with light.
O Sage, as a lord, you have seized the wheel of the sun by your might.
Bring Kutsa, the slayer of Śuṣṇa, with the horses of Vāta; for most powerful is your intoxication, and most splendid is your mental power.
As the slayer of Vṛtra and the finder of wide space, may you consider yourself the greatest winner of horses.
Just as you were for the ancient singers, O Indra—like water for one who thirsts—you have become [our refuge]. Following that very invocation, I call upon you repeatedly.
Intoxicate us for the sake of better fortune; O Indu, enter Indra as a bull.
Roaring in his fury, you pursue the enemy; you find no one to withstand you.
Settle our songs of praise within him who alone moves among the people.
Like a bull that has plowed the barley, he is nourished by his own inherent power.
In whose two hands are all the treasures of the five peoples;
seize him who is hostile toward us and strike him down like a thunderbolt from heaven!
Slay the one who does not press the soma, the one who is difficult to overcome, he who is no source of joy for you.
Grant us the knowledge of this; even a wise patron desires it.
You, O Indu, have protected him of double strength in his hymns, you who are ever-present at the summit.
In the battle, O Indu, you protected Indra, the prize-winner, in the contests for booty.
As [you did] for the ancients...
The bull among men, the king of the peoples, Indra, much-invoked, who fills the dwellings—
being praised and seeking glory, come hither to me with help, having yoked your two vigorous bay steeds.
O Indra, those bulls of yours, the stallions yoked by prayer, the coursers with their mighty chariots—mount them! Come hither with them; we invoke you, O Indra, when the Soma is pressed.
Mount the bull-like chariot; for you, the bull, the Soma is pressed and the sweet juices are poured out.
Yoking your two stallions, O Bull among the dwellers of the earth, come hither with your bay steeds down the steep slope toward me.

This sacrifice goes to the gods; this is the sacrificial food, these are the prayers, and here, O Indra, is the Soma. The sacred grass is strewn; come, O Śakra, sit upon it and drink; unyoke your two bay horses here.
O Indra, well-praised, come hither toward the sacred formulations (*brahmāṇi*) of the poet Mānya. May we, singing, find your protection at the break of dawn.
For that readiness of yours, O Indra, which exists—by which you have become a helper for those who sing your praises.
Do not consume our desire as it grows; may I obtain all [the blessings] from you, the master of life.
O Indra, King, let them not deceive us, whatever the two sisters shall do in the womb.
Even the waters have sped toward him with swift motion; may Indra come to us for friendship and strength.
Indra is the victor with his men, a hero in battles; he hears the cry of the singer who implores him.
He brings his chariot near to the donor, when he himself raises his songs.
Thus Indra, through his men, has become renowned for his glory; he is the devourer of nourishment for those who are allied with Mitra.
In the assembly, in the contest for food, the all-effecting one is praised as the singer of the sacrificer’s hymn.
O Maghavan Indra, with you we shall overcome our enemies who think themselves great. You are our protector; you are our strengthener. ...be abundant.
I have endured many autumns, wearying myself through nights and mornings that bring old age.
Old age diminishes the beauty of our bodies; may even our wives now come to us as husbands. For even those who were formerly guardians of the *ṛta* spoke truths together with the gods.
Even they, seeking help, have attained their desire; let them now unite with their mates through the bulls.
Not in vain is the toil for which the gods grant aid; may we overcome all our rivals. Here let us proclaim the hundred-pathed race, where we two, as a harmonious pair, have run together.
Desire came upon me from the obstructing river; born from here, from yonder, or from somewhere else.
Lopāmudrā leads forth the bull; the wise one suckles the unwise, the panting one.
I address this Soma, drunk within my heart, as being right here.
Whatever offense we have committed against them, may they forgive us; for mortal man has many desires.
Agastya, digging with his spades while desiring offspring, progeny, and strength—both classes he, the fierce seer, nourished; he attained true blessings among the gods.
Your well-governed horses traverse the realms when your chariot speeds around the waters.
Your golden fellies scatter spray as you drink of the sweetness; you accompany the dawns.
You two protect the one who is beyond this world, the manly one who is worthy of sacrifice, even when he is far away.
When your sister, praised by all, brings [the offering] for you both, she seeks you for strength and for the drinking of the honeyed draught.
You two placed the milk within the raw cow; you brought down the ancient [milk] from the cow who was yet uncooked.
When the one who shines with truth, like a bright ladle, offers the oblation between the wooden vessels, he worships you both.
You two indeed chose for Atri the honeyed *gharma*, like a flood of water, in your desire for it.
O Aśvins, heroes, that [offering] of yours for the sake of cattle comes toward you like the wheels of a chariot, full of sweetness.
O wonder-workers, may I turn you both toward giving with my gift of a cow, as the aged son of Tugra did.
The waters and the two worlds attend upon you with greatness; your swift razor-edged bolt, O worshipful ones, is worn away by its own impetuous force.
When you, O bounteous givers, yoke your teams of horses, you release the abundance of wealth through your inherent powers.
Like the wind, the patron rushes and hastens; like one of holy vows, he has received great strength for the sake of the sacrifice.
For we indeed, as your singers, truly celebrate you both; the niggardly man who seeks to withhold has been cast down.
And so, O blameless Aśvins, you protect Antideva, O bulls.
For you indeed, O Aśvins, day after day, [stand by him] at the winning of the flowing stream of Rudra.
Agastya, the most praised among men, awakens with thousands like the shaker of the prison-house.
When you two travel forth with the greatness of your chariot, you move swiftly like the Hotṛ-priest of man.
Bestow upon our patrons, O Nāsatyas, wealth consisting of fine horses; may we be possessors of riches.
O Aśvins, we invoke today with hymns that chariot of yours, which is most worthy of our praise for its auspicious journey—
the chariot with uninjured fellies, traveling across the heavens.
When, O most beloved ones, you two, acting as Adhvaryu priests, pour forth the waters of these most cherished riches?
This sacrifice has offered praise to you two, O dispensers of wealth, protectors of men. May your pure, water-drinking horses— divine coursers with the speed of the wind,
swift as thought, vigorous, and smooth-backed— bring you, the self-ruling Aśvins, hither.
May your chariot, like a rushing torrent, come with its smooth-seated frame for our prosperity—
your chariot that stands upon the two bulls, swifter than thought, which is foremost and worthy of worship. Born here and there,
you have both lowed together with bodies free from blemish and with your own names.
The victorious Vāmana is the patron of the great sacrifice; the other, the blessed son of Heaven, is esteemed as a lord.
May your tawny-hued, towering steed, moving downward according to our desires, come to our dwellings.
The two bay steeds of the other are nourished with strength; O Aśvins, they stir the regions with their neighing sounds.
The autumnal bull, like a conqueror, moves forth for you both, sending out many refreshments of honeyed food.
By the movements and the strengths of the other [soma], they have caused [the waters] to swell; the rushing rivers have come to us, rising upward.
A mature song has been released for you by the wise one, O Aśvins, flowing threefold even upon the firm ground.

O you two who are praised with hymns, protect us as we implore you; on your journey, hear my invocation. And may this song of yours, radiant and beautiful, nourish the men in the assembly where the triple sacred grass is spread.
O powerful ones, your bull-like cloud has swelled like a cow at the time of milking, bestowing gifts upon mankind.

O Aśvins, like Pūṣan, the bringer of abundance, the one possessing oblations awakens Agni as if at dawn; when I, praising you with my desire for wide space, invoke you both. This ritual order has come into being; now attend to it well! O sages, rejoice in the chariot that brings strength.

O inspirers of the prayer, you who are worthy of devotion, who possess the wealth of Viśpalā, sons of Heaven, pure in your vows for the sake of the righteous man— For you, O wise ones, are most like Indra, most like Maruts, most wondrous in your deeds, the best of charioteers among those who drive the chariot.
You two carry a full chariot laden with sweetness; with that, O Aśvins, you come to the donor.
O wonder-workers, what do you do here? What do you sit for? Whatever person exalts himself without an oblation—pass over him!
Strike down the life of the stingy usurer; create light for the inspired singer who utters his hymns.
Crush the dogs on both sides as they rush forward; slay the adversaries—the Aśvins have understood these things.

Make every word of the singer rich in treasure; O Nāsatyas, protect my hymn of praise. You two fashioned for yourselves this boat upon the rivers, provided with a soul and furnished with wings, for the sake of the fierce one. With which mind you two sent it forth among the gods, you flew well-winged from the great mass of water.
Taugrya was cast down into the waters, abandoned in the darkness where there is no support;
four ships, beloved by Jaṭhara, sent forth by the Aśvins, carry him across. What tree indeed stands fixed in the midst of the ocean, which Taugrya, when he was in distress, embraced?
Like the feathers of a winged bird, you two, O Aśvins, took hold [of it] and carried it away for the sake of glory.
O heroes, O Nāsatyas, may that hymn which the Mānas have uttered for you be effective today from this Soma-offering seat.
From this very place, from the Soma-rich assembly, [may we...]

Yoke that [chariot] which is swifter than thought, O mighty ones—that which has three seats and three wheels—wherewith you come to the dwelling of the doer of good deeds; with its triple-layered wings, fly like birds.
The well-rolling chariot moves as it approaches the earth; when you two, possessed of wisdom, stand ready for the strengthening food.

May this beautiful song attend to your form; O two daughters of heaven, you attend to the Dawn. Mount the well-rolling chariot that moves according to your laws, laden with oblations. Upon it, O Nāsatyas, you travel to provide sustenance for the man who desires offspring and for himself.

Let not the wolf nor the she-wolf dare to seize you; do not avoid us, nor let [the enemy] consume us. This portion is set out for you, this song, O Wonder-Workers; here are your vessels of honeyed draughts.
Gotama, Purumīḷha, and Atri, bearing oblations, call upon you both, O Wonder-Workers, for protection.
Like one who goes straight toward a pointed-out direction, O Nāsatyas, come to my invocation.
We have crossed to the further shore of this darkness; our hymn of praise has been offered to you both, O Aśvins.
Come hither by the paths traveled by the gods.

Let us invoke you both today and tomorrow at the dawning of the radiant dawn with our hymns, O Nāsatyas, you who are the bearers [of the sacrifice]. Wherever you may be, O sons of Heaven, most bountiful protectors, come for the sake of the liberal giver.
O mighty ones, rejoice well among us; slay the Paṇis while delighting in the flowing wave of Soma.
I have heard the words of those who speak with inspired thoughts; O heroes, you are the seekers and perceivers with your ears.
For glory, O Pūṣan, like two gods who have performed a service, the Nāsatyas brought the bridal procession of Sūryā.
Your lofty steeds, born in the waters, move along like the worn-out ages of the mighty Varuṇa.
O lovers of sweetness, may that gift of yours be with us; further the hymn of the poet Mānya.

When people, seeking glory, offer praise to you both for the sake of noble heroism, O bounteous givers. This hymn has been fashioned for you, O Aśvins, by the Mānas with well-turned verses, O lords of wealth.
Come, O Nāsatyas, to our home for the sake of our offspring and ourselves, rejoicing in the dwelling of Agastya.
We have crossed over...
Which of these two is the earlier, which the later? How were they born? O sages, who truly knows?

By their own self, they support the universe; indeed, the two days and nights roll apart like two wheels. The two footless ones, moving much, bear as their offspring the many-footed moving germ, as a son in the lap of his parents; O Heaven and Earth, protect us from evil.
I invoke the unassailable gift of Aditi, which is free from distress, heavenly, inviolable, and accompanied by homage.
O Heaven and Earth, bring that forth for the singer!
May we follow those two worlds, the parents of the gods, who do not suffer from heat and who provide protection with their aid.
Both [worlds], by means of both kinds of days, [attend] the gods; Heaven and Earth...
Meeting together, young, with common borders, two sisters, kinswomen in the lap of their parents;
Kissing the navel of the world, Heaven and Earth...
The two wide, great, and lofty abodes, the parents of the gods, I invoke with the *ṛta* and with the protection of the gods— those two of beautiful countenance who bestow immortality.
The two wide, broad, vast, and far-reaching ones, I address with reverence at this sacrifice.
May Heaven and Earth, who bestow good fortune and great victory, [grant us their favor].
Whatever offense we have committed against the gods, or against our friend, or even against the lord of the house, may this prayer be a means of appeasement for them;
O Heaven and Earth...
May both noble praises protect me; may both assist me with their aid and favor. O gods, being well-pleased, may we enjoy abundant food from the most liberal patron.
I, the wise one, have proclaimed this Truth to Heaven and Earth so that it may be heard far and wide for the first time.
May they two protect us from reproach and from misfortune in the encounter; may the father and the mother guard us with their aids.
O Heaven and Earth, may this be true, as I address you here, O Father and Mother: be present with your protections, O lowest [nearest] of the gods, so that we may know...

May the god Savitṛ, the lord of all men, come to our sacrifice with his praises and his blessings. May you, O youthful ones, gladden us with your wisdom at the time of the day’s close, so that the whole world may rejoice. May all the gods come to us together—Mitra, Aryaman, and Varuṇa, in harmony.

So that all may become our strengtheners, making us victorious and not like one whose power is wavering. I praise with hymns Agni, your dearest guest, you who are victorious and well-disposed toward us, so that Varuṇa may be our glorious fame, and the lord, praised by the enemy, may bring us nourishment across [all difficulties].
I approach you both with homage, O Dawn and Night, who strive for victory, like a cow easy to milk; measuring out the hymn on the same day, in the diverse forms within that single udder.
And may Ahi Budhnya bring us joy; like a mother swelling with milk for her child, the river flows toward us.
By which we may urge on the offspring of the waters, whom the stallions swift as thought carry hither;
and may Tvaṣṭṛ come toward us here, in harmony with the patrons at the time of the feast.
May Indra, the slayer of Vṛtra, the filler of the peoples, the most eminent among men, come hither.
And our hymns, like mares yoked for the chariot, lick him as cows lick their young calf. Our songs have approached him, the most fragrant of men, as wives approach their husband.
And may the Maruts, with their swelling hosts, together with Rodasī, sit down with us in one accord.
With spotted horses, they are like chariots; they are the destroyers of enemies, like gods bound by friendship.
When they have manifested themselves through their greatness, they yoke their teams with a perfect hymn of praise. Then, as if on a fair day, their weapons drench the entire enemy host with moisture.
Bring forward the Aśvins for our protection; bring forward Pūṣan, for they possess their own inherent power.
Viṣṇu is free from malice, as are Vāta and Ṛbhukṣan; may I turn the gods hitherward for the sake of favor.
O worshipful ones, this is that prayer of ours for you—filling us with strength and providing a seat for us once again.
RV 1.186.11.2: He who, seeking wealth, strives among the gods...
RV 1.187.01.1: Now I shall praise food, the great ordinance, the power;
RV 1.187.01.2: by whose might Trita shattered Vṛtra limb from limb.
O sweet Soma, O honeyed food, we have chosen thee;
be our protector. Come to us, O food, as a benefactor with thy auspicious aids.
Bringing bliss, not to be hated, a friend most kind and free from duplicity.
O *pitu*, these juices of yours are spread throughout the realms, resting in heaven like the winds.

These [gifts] of yours, O *pitu*, are given; yours, O most sweet *pitu*, are they. The flavors of juices, like those with powerful necks, hasten forward in their sweetness. In you, O *pitu*, the mind of the great gods is placed.
A beautiful deed was performed with your banner; O Ahi-han, you have slain the serpent.
O Food, when you went there to the radiant heights of the mountains, even there, O Food of sweetness, come to us sufficiently for our enjoyment.
Whatever essence of the waters and the plants we extract, O Vāta, become fatness for us.
O Soma, whatever portion of yours we enjoy that is mixed with milk, mixed with barley— [grant us prosperity].
O Vātāpi...
O herb, become a gruel-porridge, fat, kidney-shaped, and swelling; O Vātāpi...
O *pitu*, we have refined you with our words, as cattle refine their offerings;
you who provide a feast for the gods, you who provide a feast for us.
Enkindled today, you shine as a god among the gods, O conqueror of thousands.
As a messenger, as a sage, carry the oblations.
O Tanūnapāt, for him who walks the path of Truth, the sacrifice is adorned with honey;
may he bestow thousandfold nourishments.
Being invoked and worthy of praise, bring here for us the gods who are worthy of sacrifice;
O Agni, you are the winner of thousands.
Spreading eastward with might the sacrificial grass that brings a thousand heroes, he has strewn it.
Where you Ādityas shine forth, there the doors— resplendent,
sovereign, pervasive, powerful, many, and more than many— have poured forth streams of clarified butter.
For, adorned with beautiful gold and fine ornaments, the two Dawns shine forth in splendor; may those two Dawns sit here in this dwelling.
For they are the first of the two divine Hotṛ-priests, the sages of eloquent speech.
May Bhāratī, Iḷā, and Sarasvatī— whomsoever among you I here invoke— perform this sacrifice for us;
may they impel us toward glory.
For Tvaṣṭṛ, the lord, has fashioned all forms and all cattle;
sacrifice for us so that there may be abundance of them.
O Vanaspati, by your own power, release the path for the gods.
May Agni make the oblations sweet.
Agni, the leader of the gods, is adorned with the Gāyatra hymn;
he shines forth at the utterances of Svāhā.
O Agni, lead us by a good path to wealth, O God who knowest all ways.
Drive away from us the sin that leads astray; we shall offer unto thee the most abundant speech of adoration.
O Agni, as one new, do thou carry us across all difficulties with blessings.
Be wide, abundant, and spacious for us; grant well-being and security to our children and descendants.
O Agni, drive away from us all maladies; let those who offer no protection against fire attack the surrounding peoples.
O worshipful God, together with all the immortals, restore to us the earth for our prosperity.
Protect us, O Agni, with your unfailing protections, shining brightly in your beloved dwelling.
O youngest one, may no fear reach your singer now, nor in the future, O powerful one.
Do not deliver us, O Agni, to the malevolent, to the greedy enemy, or to misfortune.
Do not deliver us to one who is greedy, nor to one who bites, nor to one who seeks to harm us, O Lord of Might!
O Agni, born of Truth, may one such as you, when praised, grant protection to our bodies. For you, O God, are the discerning one who drives away all those who wish to injure or revile us.

O Agni, you who know both kinds, you approach those men at the onset of the sacrifice, O worshipful one. At the conclusion of the rite, you become one to be commanded by Manu; like a draft-ox, you are to be groomed by the eager priests.
We have uttered our secret words within this victorious Agni, the son of Māna.
May we, together with the thousand seers, win... [the prize].

With new hymns, magnify Bṛhaspati—the unassailable bull, whose tongue is sweet, who is worthy of song, and who shines brightly; he whose praises the gods and mortals alike listen to as they are being uttered.
To him, the seasonal hymns of praise resort—he who was released like a surge of those seeking the gods.
For Bṛhaspati, being straight and pervasive, became Mātariśvan in accordance with the *ṛta*.
He extends his arms forth like Savitṛ, fashioning the song of praise, the lifting of homage, and the verse of fame.
By his wisdom, he who is to be honored on the day of sacrifice is like a terrifying beast, powerful and free from malice.

His fame resounds across heaven and earth; like a swift steed, he, the wise possessor of wealth, moves forward. Like the weapons of wild beasts, these [songs] of Bṛhaspati go forth toward the heavens that dispel the serpent-like darkness.

Those wicked Pajras who, regarding you as a mere domestic animal, live off your bounty—O Bṛhaspati, you do not bestow wealth upon the evil-minded; rather, you consume the one who hates the sacred word.
Like a path easy to travel that leads to good pasture, he is like a beloved friend who is difficult to restrain.
Those who are irresistible and look upon us have stood there, uncovering what was veiled. To him the hymns go together like rivers, like streams with banks and wheels rushing toward the ocean.
The wise Bṛhaspati, the vulture, beholds both from within: the waters and the crossing.
Thus has the great, many-born, and mighty Bṛhaspati been established as the bull-god.
May he, being praised, bestow upon us wealth consisting of heroes and cattle.
The *kaṅkata* bird, the *kaṅkata*, and also the *satīnakaṅkata*.
"Two," "two," "gnats"—thus she was seen; she has smeared herself.
Coming, she kills the unseen; going away, she also kills.
Furthermore, striking, she kills; furthermore, grinding, she grinds.
The *śarāsa*, *kuśarāsa*, *darbha*, and *sairya* grasses, as well as the *mauñja*, *adṛṣṭa*, and *vairiṇa*—all these together have sought to bite.
The cows have settled in the cow-pen; the wild animals have entered their lairs.
The spies of men have been seen; the unseen ones have been caught. These very ones have appeared like thieves at nightfall;
you who were unseen have now become seen by all, and you have been discovered.
Heaven is your father, Earth your mother, Soma your brother, and Aditi your sister.
Unseen yet seen by all, stand still and rest well!
Those that are on the shoulders, those that are on the limbs, those that are needle-like, and those that are prickly—[drive them away].
"Unseen ones, vanish all together from here; nothing at all shall remain for you.
The Sun rises in the east, seen by all, the slayer of the unseen.
Crushing all the unseen spirits and all the female sorceresses."
There has that Sun flown up, consuming many things;
the Āditya, visible from all mountains, is the destroyer of the unseen.
I place the poison in the Sun, like a leather bag in the house of a liquor-drinker.
He indeed shall not die; may we not die. The one who stands upon his bay horses has made your poison honey-sweet.
This tiny little bird has swallowed your poison. He indeed shall not die...
Three times seven sparks have eaten the blossom of the poison. Even they do not die from it, nor do we...
Of the ninety-nine [stems] that cause the poison to grow—
O enemy, seize the foremost name of all these [plants] which belongs to him...
Three times seven are the peahens; there are seven sisters who are maidens.
They have carried away your poison, like women carrying water in jars.
So small is the *kuṣumbhaka* worm; I shatter its shell with a stone.
From there the poison has flowed away, following the distant enclosures.
As it was rolling down from the mountain, the *kuṣumbhaka* spoke thus.
O scorpion, your venom is sapless; O scorpion, your venom is a tasteless poison.
